lesson.title: Plotting a Signal's Harmonics on the Frequency Axis
lesson.summary: A frequency spectrum is a plot of a signal's harmonic amplitudes against frequency, turning a table of Fourier coefficients into a picture you can read at a glance.
lesson.body:
A list of Fourier coefficients, a1, b1, a2, b2, and so on, is correct but hard to absorb at a glance. The frequency spectrum fixes that by plotting amplitude on the vertical axis against frequency on the horizontal axis. Because a periodic signal only contains energy at the fundamental frequency and its exact integer multiples (its harmonics), that plot is not a smooth curve but a series of vertical lines, one at each harmonic frequency, with height equal to that harmonic's amplitude. This is often called a line spectrum for exactly that reason: everywhere between the lines, the amplitude is exactly zero, because a periodic signal simply has no energy at non-harmonic frequencies.

Building one is direct once you have the harmonic content from the Fourier series. Mark the horizontal axis in hertz at f0, 2f0, 3f0, 4f0 and so on. At each marked frequency, draw a vertical line whose height is that harmonic's amplitude. If a particular harmonic's coefficient came out to zero, as happens for every even harmonic of a square wave, you simply leave that position blank. The empty gaps are just as informative as the lines themselves: a spectrum with nothing at the even harmonics is an instant visual signature of a certain kind of waveform, long before you have to reread a table of numbers.

Continuing the square wave example from the Harmonic Content chapter: a 10 V peak, 1 kHz square wave produces a frequency spectrum with a line at 1 kHz reaching 12.73 V, a shorter line at 3 kHz reaching 4.24 V, a shorter one still at 5 kHz reaching 2.55 V, one at 7 kHz reaching 1.82 V, and absolutely nothing at 2 kHz, 4 kHz, or 6 kHz. If you sketch this on graph paper, the lines trace out a smooth 1/n envelope that gets sparser and lower as you move right, with every other slot empty. That shape, tall odd lines and empty even slots decaying like 1/n, is the frequency spectrum's way of encoding everything the Harmonic Content chapter described in words.

The frequency axis itself comes straight from the Frequency prerequisite: each harmonic sits at an exact integer multiple of f0 = 1/T. In practice, engineers use the frequency spectrum to check very concrete things: does any harmonic of a switching regulator's clock fall inside a sensitive receiver band, does a motor drive's output spectrum stay within the harmonics an input filter is rated to attenuate, does an audio signal's energy stay inside the 20 Hz to 20 kHz range a system needs to reproduce. All of those questions are awkward to answer from a table of an and bn values but nearly instant to answer by eye once the same information is drawn as a frequency spectrum.
